title: Pascal's Triangle
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing factorials versus building each row from the one above, then a multiplicative shortcut within a single row.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given numRows, build the first numRows rows of Pascal's triangle, where every row starts and ends with 1 and every other value is the sum of the two values above it.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Combinatorial values, binomial coefficients, with a much cheaper recursive or incremental relationship hiding underneath the factorial definition."],["Difficulty","Beginner"],["Tags","Math, Dynamic Programming"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing that factorial recomputation is wasteful, applying the row-from-previous-row recurrence, and knowing the further multiplicative single-row shortcut."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a number numRows, build the first numRows rows of Pascal's triangle. Every row starts and ends with 1, and every other value is the sum of the two numbers directly above it in the previous row.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Bean Machine Counting Paths
blocks.text: Picture a bean machine (a board of pegs a ball bounces through) where a ball dropped from the very top can bounce either left or right at every peg it hits. The number written at any position in Pascal's triangle is exactly the number of different paths a ball could take to land at that exact spot. A position can only be reached from the two positions diagonally above it, one reached by bouncing left and one by bouncing right, which is exactly why each value is the sum of the two values above.

blocks.caption: Every value is the sum of the two values above it

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: numRows = 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Values","Why"],"rows":[["0","1","The very first row is always just a single 1, nothing above it to sum."],["1","1, 1","Both edge values are always 1 by definition, and this row is short enough that both positions are edges."],["2","1, 2, 1","The middle value, 2, is the sum of the two 1s directly above it in row 1."],["3","1, 3, 3, 1","Each middle value, 3 and 3, comes from adding a 1 and a 2 from row 2."],["4","1, 4, 6, 4, 1","Each interior value continues the same pattern, summing the two values diagonally above it in row 3."]]}

blocks.text: Row 2's middle value, 2, is the sum of the two 1s directly above it in row 1. Row 3's middle values, 3 and 3, each come from adding a 1 and a 2 from row 2.
Example: numRows = 1
Only the very first row is needed, which is always just [1], with nothing above it to sum.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about how much of the combinatorial definition is actually needed.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every value in Pascal's triangle has an exact combinatorial formula, a binomial coefficient, but that formula requires computing three separate factorials from scratch for every single cell.

Observation 2: The same triangle also has a much simpler recursive definition built directly into the problem: every interior value is just the sum of the two values directly above it in the previous row.

Observation 3: If the previous row is already known, building the next row only requires simple additions, no factorials, no large multiplications, no recomputation of anything already solved.

Observation 4: Going one step further, even within a single row, each value can be built from just the one value immediately before it, using a small multiplicative relationship, meaning the entire previous row does not even need to be kept in memory.
That reasoning alone already lays out the whole path: skip the factorials, build row from row, then shrink even that down to one running value per row.
6. Brute Force Solution

The most literal approach is to compute every single value directly from its combinatorial definition: the value at row r, position c equals r factorial divided by (c factorial times (r minus c) factorial), recomputing all three factorials from scratch for every cell.
Step by step algorithm

items: For each row from 0 up to numRows minus 1.
For each position in that row, compute the row factorial, the position factorial, and the (row minus position) factorial.
Divide to get the binomial coefficient for that exact cell.
Collect all rows into the final triangle.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recompute three factorials for every single cell

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: factorial is written as its own small helper function since it is called three separate times per cell, once for the row, once for the column, once for row minus column, and writing that loop three times inline would be repetitive.

The binomial function divides by both factorial(col) and factorial(row minus col) together, matching the exact mathematical nCr formula, rather than dividing by one and then the other in separate steps, since dividing at the wrong point could truncate incorrectly.

Every single cell independently recomputes its own three factorials from scratch, with nothing carried over between cells, which is deliberately the least efficient part of this version and exactly what the next section removes.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because the binomial coefficient formula is a mathematically exact description of every value in Pascal's triangle, so computing it directly always gives the correct answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: roughly O(numRows cubed), since there are about numRows squared cells, and computing a factorial from scratch for each one costs up to O(numRows) work.
Space: O(numRows squared) for the output triangle itself, which is unavoidable since every value must be returned.

Limitation: recomputing factorials from scratch for every cell is wasteful, since Pascal's triangle has a much simpler recursive definition, each value is just the sum of two already known values from the row directly above, no factorials required at all.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recomputing factorials from scratch works but is wasteful: nearly all of that factorial computation duplicates work already done for a neighboring cell in the same or an adjacent row.

What Pascal's triangle's own definition already gives for free: a direct recurrence, every interior value is simply the sum of the two values directly above it, no factorials involved at all.

Can a row be built using only the previous row's already computed values: yes, since every interior value's two dependencies live entirely in the row directly above it.

What about the edge values: they are always 1 by definition, no computation or lookup needed for them at all.

The core idea: build the triangle row by row, reusing the previous row's values directly instead of recomputing anything from factorials.

Instead of the combinatorial formula, use the recurrence relation directly: every row can be built from the previous row alone, since the value at any interior position is simply the sum of the two values above it.
The optimization is to build the triangle row by row, reusing the previous row's already computed values instead of recomputing anything from scratch.
9. Optimized Solution
Start each new row filled with 1s at both edges. For every interior position, set its value to the sum of the two neighboring values from the previous row.
Dry run for row 4, given row 3 = [1, 3, 3, 1]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Position","Computation","Value","Why"],"rows":[["0","Edge","1","The first position in every row is always 1 by definition, never computed from a sum."],["1","1 (row 3, pos 0) + 3 (row 3, pos 1)","4","An interior value sums the two positions diagonally above it in the previous row."],["2","3 (row 3, pos 1) + 3 (row 3, pos 2)","6","Same rule applied at the next position."],["3","3 (row 3, pos 2) + 1 (row 3, pos 3)","4","Same rule applied again."],["4","Edge","1","The last position in every row is also always 1 by definition."]]}

blocks.text: Row 4 comes out to [1, 4, 6, 4, 1], matching the known triangle exactly.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build each row directly from the row above, no factorials at all

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because Pascal's triangle's defining rule, stated directly in the problem, is exactly this recurrence: every interior value equals the sum of the two values diagonally above it. Building row by row and reading directly from the already-finished previous row is simply applying that rule literally, with no need to re-derive it through factorials, since the previous row already is the correct set of values to sum from.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["Position is the first or last in its row","Set directly to 1, no lookup or addition needed","The row's two edge values"],["Position is anywhere in the interior of the row","Set to the sum of the value directly above and the value above and to the left, both read from the already completed previous row","The correct interior value, matching the combinatorial formula exactly"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Each new row starts pre-filled entirely with 1s, which already correctly handles both edge positions before the inner loop even runs, since it only needs to overwrite the interior positions.
The inner loop only touches positions from 1 up to row minus 1, deliberately skipping the two edges that are already correctly set to 1.

The previous row is indexed directly to read its values, relying on every previous row already being fully built and stored before the current row starts, which is guaranteed by processing rows strictly in order from 0 upward.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(numRows squared), one addition per cell, matching the size of the output exactly, this is already optimal since every value must be produced.
Space: O(numRows squared) for the output, plus needing to keep the full previous row around to reference while building the next one.
10. Further Optimization: Building a Row Without the Row Above

The optimized solution still needs the entire previous row sitting in memory to build the next one. There is a way to build a row using only the single value that came right before it in the same row, using a multiplicative version of the binomial coefficient relationship: each value equals the one before it in the row, multiplied by (row minus position plus 1), divided by position.
Dry run for row 4

blocks.content: {"headers":["Position","Computation","Value","Why"],"rows":[["0","Starting value","1","Every row begins with a 1, the seed value the rest of the row is built from."],["1","1 times (4 minus 1 plus 1) over 1","4","The multiplicative ratio produces the next value using only the previous one in this same row."],["2","4 times (4 minus 2 plus 1) over 2","6","Same multiplicative step repeated, still no reference to any other row."],["3","6 times (4 minus 3 plus 1) over 3","4","Same step again."],["4","4 times (4 minus 4 plus 1) over 4","1","The final value in the row, arriving back at 1 exactly as expected."]]}

blocks.text: The same row, [1, 4, 6, 4, 1], is produced without ever looking at row 3's values at all, only using the value immediately before it in row 4 itself.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: each value only needs the one before it in the same row

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The multiplicative step, value times (row minus col plus 1) divided by col, is a rearranged form of the ratio between two consecutive binomial coefficients in the same row.
Multiplication happens before division in that expression specifically to avoid truncating a fractional intermediate result, since dividing too early can silently produce a wrong final value.

value is carried forward as a single running variable across the whole row, rather than being read from any stored previous row, which is exactly what removes the need to keep an entire extra row of data in memory.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(numRows squared), the same as before, matching the output size.
Space: still O(numRows squared) for the required output, but no longer needs the entire previous row kept around as extra reference data, only a single running value, a genuine reduction in auxiliary bookkeeping.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is recognizing that a value defined combinatorially (factorials and binomial coefficients) often has an equivalent, much cheaper recursive or incremental relationship. Moving from factorials, to referencing the row above, to referencing only the previous value in the same row, is a natural ladder of increasingly minimal dependencies.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the edge values of 1 at the start and end of every row.
Off by one errors when indexing into the previous row while building interior values.
Integer overflow with the factorial or multiplicative approaches on larger rows, where a wider integer type is safer.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["numRows = 1","Returns just [[1]], the single first row, with nothing to sum at all."],["The very first and last position of every row","Always exactly 1, and never computed from a sum, regardless of how large the row is."],["Larger numRows values","Factorial based approaches risk integer overflow well before either recurrence based approach does, since factorials grow far faster than the triangle's own values."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is a great opportunity to connect combinatorics (binomial coefficients) with dynamic programming (building each row from the last). Mentioning both the row-to-row recurrence and the single-value multiplicative shortcut shows a layered understanding rather than only knowing one way to build the triangle.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid recomputing factorials", think: build each row directly from the row above using the sum recurrence.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid storing the whole previous row", think: the multiplicative single-value relationship within one row.
If the interviewer says "why does the brute force cost more", think: it repeats the same factorial computation across many cells instead of reusing already known values.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why is O(numRows squared) an unavoidable lower bound for both time and space here, regardless of algorithm?
Can you compute a single specific value, like row 20, position 10, without building the rest of the triangle at all?
How would you avoid integer overflow if numRows were allowed to be much larger?
Can you build the triangle using only O(numRows) space at any one time, discarding rows no longer needed?
What is the relationship between the multiplicative single-row shortcut and the original binomial coefficient formula?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any dynamic programming problem where each row or state is built entirely from the row or state directly before it, the same "keep only what is needed from the previous step" idea.
Binomial coefficient and combinatorics problems in general, where a factorial based definition often hides a cheaper additive or multiplicative recurrence.
Space optimized DP, where an entire table collapses down to just the previous row, or even a single rolling value, once the true dependency is understood.
Pascal's Triangle II, a single specific row requested directly, which builds naturally on this same multiplicative single-row technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three approaches must produce O(numRows squared) output values, which sets a hard floor on both time and space. The brute force adds an extra unnecessary factor from recomputing factorials. Both recurrence based approaches reach the optimal O(numRows squared) time, with the multiplicative version additionally avoiding the need to retain the entire previous row as extra reference data.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: combinatorial values, binomial coefficients, with a much cheaper recursive or incremental relationship than their original factorial-based definition.

Core Idea: every interior value is the sum of the two values directly above it in the previous row, and going further, every value within a row can be built from just the one value before it using a small multiplicative relationship.
Time: O(numRows cubed) for the brute force, O(numRows squared) for both recurrence based versions, matching the unavoidable output size.
Space: O(numRows squared) for the output across all versions; the further optimized version additionally avoids keeping an entire extra row as reference data.

Most Important Observation: factorials, row-above recurrence, and single-row multiplicative recurrence are three increasingly minimal descriptions of the exact same values, each removing one more layer of unnecessary dependency.
Interview Difficulty: easy to state correctly with factorials, but recognizing and applying the cheaper recurrences is what turns a slow answer into an optimal one.
One line memory trick: each value is the sum of the two above it, or the previous value times a small ratio, never a fresh factorial.
